name: Distal Biceps Tendinopathy
subtitle: 12-Week Loading Program

governingRule.headline: Everything is gated by one signal: how the arm feels the next morning.
rows: Same as or better than baseline
notes: The 24-hour response is the one that decides. Pain during loading is expected and is not damage.
Pain that is worse the following morning means the dose was too high - repeat the previous week rather than progressing.
Both arms get the same program at independent loads. Never let the better arm set the dose for the worse one.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Isometrics
phases.purpose: Reduce pain, begin restoring tendon load tolerance without range-of-motion stress.

blocks.title: Isometric Elbow Flexion Hold
cues: Seated, upper arm against your side, elbow bent to 90 degrees.
Forearm neutral (thumb up) if supinated is provocative; move to palm-up once tolerable.
Push up against something immovable - underside of a desk, a rack pin, a fixed bar, your other hand.
Build tension over 2 seconds, then hold steady.

blocks.title: Isometric Supination Hold
cues: Elbow at 90 degrees, hold a hammer or a dumbbell gripped at one end.
Rotate toward palm-up until you feel resistance, hold static against gravity.

criteria.label: Morning baseline pain reduced from starting point
No next-morning flare for 4 consecutive days

advance.note: If not met at 2 weeks, stay in Phase 1 for another week. This is common and not a setback.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Heavy Slow Resistance
phases.purpose: The main intervention. Progressive tendon loading drives collagen remodeling.
phases.tempoNote: 3 seconds up, 3 seconds down. No pause, no bounce, no swing. A set of 10 reps takes a full minute. If you cannot control the 3-second lowering, the weight is too heavy - this is the most common error and it wastes the entire session.
warmup: 5 min general - bike, rower, or brisk walk
Elbow flexion/extension through full range, no load, 2 x 15
One warm-up set of the first exercise at ~50% of working load, full tempo

exercises.title: Incline Dumbbell Curl
exercises.note: The incline (45-60 degrees) puts the biceps on stretch at the bottom, which is where the loading stimulus matters most.

exercises.title: Supinated Barbell or EZ-Bar Curl
exercises.note: One bar, one load - the right arm gates this lift. The straight bar's full supination is the target position; you need to rebuild it, not avoid it permanently.

exercises.title: Loaded Supination (Screwdriver)
exercises.note: Elbow at 90 degrees and pinned to your side. Hold a dumbbell by one end so the weight hangs to one side. Rotate palm-down to palm-up. This isolates the supination function of the distal biceps - the specific thing that hurts.

phases.repMaxNote: Rep max means the last rep is genuinely hard but the tempo holds and pain stays at 4/10 or less. Not to failure.

advance.note: Weekly load increase of roughly 5%, only if the 24-hour rule was clean all three sessions the prior week. If it wasn't, repeat the week at the same load.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Return to Loading
phases.purpose: Rebuild toward previous training loads and establish permanent maintenance.
warmup: 5 min general - bike, rower, or brisk walk
Elbow flexion/extension through full range, no load, 2 x 15
One warm-up set of the first exercise at ~50% of working load, full tempo
phases.repMaxNote: One heavy slow resistance session per week: 3 x 6, full 3s/3s tempo.
phases.maintenanceNote: One HSR session weekly, more or less indefinitely. This is the part people skip, and skipping it is the single most common reason chronic tendinopathy recurs. It costs about ten minutes.
reintroduction: Reintroduce heavy pressing progressively - add back ~10% load per week, restore full depth only after two clean weeks at full load.
Reintroduce supinated pulling (chin-ups, supinated rows) at low load, progress the same way.
Keep one heavy slow resistance session per week: 3 x 6, full 3s/3s tempo.
permanentChanges: EZ-bar or hammer curls as the default for heavy elbow flexion work; straight-bar supinated curls as accessory work at moderate load.
Capped dumbbell press depth on heavy sets.
72 hours between heavy sessions loading the same tissue.
No training to failure on elbow flexion.

flare.definition: A flare is 24-hour pain clearly worse than baseline, or a return of pain in daily activities.
steps: Do not stop entirely. Drop back to Phase 1 isometrics - 5 x 45s, twice daily.
Hold there 3-5 days, until morning baseline returns.
Resume Phase 2 at 70% of the load you flared on.
Rebuild over 2 weeks to where you were.
flare.note: Expect two or three flares across the twelve weeks. They are part of the normal course and do not mean the program failed. A flare that does not settle within a week, or that comes with new weakness, needs an exam rather than another cycle of this.

restrictions.status: Continue, but use neutral or pronated grips. Drop supinated rows and chin-ups. Reduce load ~30% initially, rebuild over the block.
Continue at reduced load (start ~50-60%) with restricted depth - stop the dumbbell descent level with the chest, not below. Rebuild toward previous loads across Phase 3.
Nothing beyond the three prescribed exercises. No additional curl variations, no training to failure on elbow flexion.

whatNotToDo.title: Rest alone
whatNotToDo.text: Reliably fails in chronic tendinopathy. The tendon is under-conditioned, not inflamed.

whatNotToDo.title: Prolonged NSAIDs
whatNotToDo.text: May blunt the adaptive response to loading. Short courses for acute flares only.

whatNotToDo.title: Corticosteroid injection
whatNotToDo.text: Short-term pain relief, worse long-term outcomes, and elevated rupture risk in load-bearing tendons.

whatNotToDo.title: Permanently avoiding supination
whatNotToDo.text: Avoidance means the tendon never adapts to the position that provokes it. The provoking movement is the rehabilitation, scaled appropriately.

whatNotToDo.title: Stretching into pain
whatNotToDo.text: Compressive stretching of an irritable tendon tends to aggravate it.

redFlags: Sudden pop, sharp tearing sensation, or visible change in muscle shape
Marked weakness in supination compared to the other side
Numbness or tingling into the forearm or hand
Pain that no longer varies with load, or night pain
Flare that does not settle within one week of returning to isometrics
timeline: First noticeable reduction in daily pain
Longer end of every range above
timelineNote: Progress is non-linear. A plateau of two to three weeks mid-block is normal. A plateau of six to eight weeks with no change is the point to seek imaging.
beforeStarting: The bilateral pattern and multi-year history are the two features that justify an in-person exam first - to grade the tendon, exclude a partial tear that would change the progression, and screen for systemic contributors. This program is written to be handed to a physio or sports med physician and modified, not run blind.
